The findings suggest that biological signs of brain aging may appear decades before obvious symptoms and could eventually make the gut a target for prevention.

more.summary: In front of most Australian houses, between the sidewalk and the road, runs a strip of land most people never really think about. In Australia, it's called the nature strip, but it goes by other names in other regions, including a verge, parkway or tree lawn.

more.title: A climate threat may lurk beneath Antarctica's last great unknown
more.summary: A region of Antarctica with some of the greatest potential to reshape the natural world and human society is also the least scientifically understood and explored.

more.title: Nanoneedle arrays map RNA in fresh tissue without sequencing or amplification
more.summary: Recently, spatial omics has become a powerful tool, enabling researchers to see not only what molecules are present in a tissue, but also where they are located and how they are organized across cells, tissue structures and local microenvironments. This spatial context has deepened our understanding of cancer, neurobiology and immunology.

more.title: Too many males to choose from can overwhelm female frogs—and change who gets to mate
more.summary: If you've ever felt overwhelmed by menu options at a restaurant, cereal varieties at the grocery store or potential partners while scrolling through dating apps, you've experienced choice overload.

more.title: Gamma-ray search sets new limits on dark matter annihilation in the inner Milky Way
more.summary: Dark matter could be a type of matter in the universe that does not emit, absorb or reflect detectable light and appears to interact very weakly with regular matter. Although physicists have observed gravitational effects attributed to dark matter, they have not yet been able to determine what it is made of.

more.title: One giant clam contains a month‑by‑month diary of the Great Barrier Reef's climate 200 years ago
more.summary: When you swim through the azure waters of the Great Barrier Reef, there is one creature on the seafloor that's almost impossible to miss: the giant clam. Its huge, fluted shell frames a soft mantle shimmering with electric blue, green and gold.

more.title: Heat-trapping gas once frozen in Arctic ground is slowly leaking and warming the planet
more.summary: As Ted Schuur stepped along the edges of Smith Lake, a bubble surfaced from the muck underfoot. And then another. They're bubbles of methane, a potent heat-trapping gas made from decomposing plants and animals that had once been stuck in Alaska's frigid permafrost. But that frozen ground is thawing because the Arctic is warming four times faster than the rest of the globe.

more.title: TechCrunch Mobility: Reining in robotaxis
more.author: Kirsten Korosec
more.summary: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.

more.title: How Enceladus' ocean spray becomes chemically diverse ice grains
more.summary: Saturn's icy moon Enceladus hides a global ocean beneath its frozen surface. From fractures near its south pole, material from this ocean is ejected into space as a plume of water vapor and ice particles. These particles offer scientists a rare opportunity to investigate an extraterrestrial ocean without drilling through kilometers of ice.

more.title: Lions and cheetahs and chimps, oh my: a spotlight on Africa's diverse wildlife
more.author: Jennifer Ouellette
more.summary: Wunmi Mosaku ( Sinners, Loki ) narrates NatGeo's new documentary Africa: Earth's Wild Home

more.title: The Rise Of Bank-Built AI, Weekly Funding Rundown & More
more.author: Team Inc42
more.summary: Banking’s AI Investment Playbook No longer content with buying AI tools, banks are moving to co-build and invest in AI…

more.title: A meteor hit Oklahoma 100 million years later than scientists thought
more.summary: A meteor crater buried beneath Oklahoma has turned out to be nearly 100 million years younger than scientists thought. Zircon crystals show the Ames impact occurred about 370 million years ago, meaning it was not part of the mysterious Ordovician bombardment once linked to a possible ring of debris around Earth. Instead, the impact coincided closely with a major mass extinction that devastated marine life.

more.title: Scientists find a surprising clue to why the universe’s expansion doesn’t add up
more.summary: Tiny magnetic fields created shortly after the Big Bang may help explain the long-running disagreement over how fast the universe is expanding. Detailed simulations show that these primordial fields could have changed the formation of hydrogen in the early universe, affecting the cosmic microwave background and the expansion rate inferred from it.

more.title: Giant fluctuations of focused light reveal hidden correlations in opaque materials
more.summary: When light travels through a strongly scattering material, such as biological tissue or other disordered opaque media, it follows many different paths and produces a seemingly random speckle pattern. Wavefront shaping makes it possible to control this complex interference and focus light through such materials.

more.title: A forgotten 30-year forest experiment just delivered a huge surprise
more.summary: A 30-year forestry experiment in Australia found that heavily thinned mountain ash forests grew unusually large trees while recovering enough carbon to match or exceed untouched areas. The results suggest carefully managed thinning could support timber production, wildlife habitat, and carbon storage at the same time.

more.title: Hungary's dwindling paprika producers battle to save signature spice
more.summary: Working from before dawn until midnight, farmers Nikoletta Pajsan Nagy and Laszlo Pajsan fought Europe's driest summer ever to save their red pepper harvest in Hungary.

more.title: Scientists just found a new way to make hydrogen from water
more.summary: A new light-activated material can efficiently produce hydrogen from water without requiring an additional expensive metal catalyst. Researchers say its unusual sulfur-based chemistry could point toward cheaper and more practical ways to turn sunlight into clean fuel.

more.title: All hail electrification. But let’s talk about the hard part.
more.author: Dan Gearino, Inside Climate News
more.summary: The IEA and climate negotiators want to set a target for shifting the economy to run on electricity.

more.title: Cry for help as French-Swiss lake dries up
more.summary: The picturesque Lac des Brenets between France and Switzerland has dried up after a record-breaking hot summer, leaving locals crying out for help to save the lake.
